### Option 1: Elevated Literary Style
*This version translates the original poetic voice into sophisticated, resonant literary prose while preserving all metaphors, imagery, and historical weight.*

> On that fateful day in December, I sat down beside the Miss Muffet of Montgomery. I was endlessly, profoundly weary. My feet were swollen from hours of stitching seams on filthy fabric, my body exhausted from pedaling a rusted Singer machine, its needle jammed with dingy cotton thread. For a lifetime, I had traversed centuries of grief, soaked in tears, all while dreaming of my own true, dignified self draped in silk. 
>
> It did not happen as the popular stories tell it. Miss Liberty Muffet did not merely leap in alarm at the sight of me. Not entirely. They dragged me away, pinning down a thousand struggling limbs. Yet the rest of me remained—an indelible cloud, a magnificent reckoning rising on the bleak December horizon, returning to sit in judgment. 
>
> How many miles are traveled as the Jim Crow flies? Across oceans and beyond. I rumbled with an undeniable force, and they could not hold me down for long. No. My feet were tired, my eyes were sore, and my heart was raw from constantly mending the soiled fringes of Miss Liberty Muffet’s garment. Yet I rode onward once more, traveling a thousand blood-soaked miles in the wake of the Crow on that December day, forever remembered, when I took my seat beside Miss Muffet of Montgomery. 
>
> I asked, as the old adage goes, “What is in the bowl, Thief?” I declared, “That is your curse,” and I said, “This is my path.” 
>
> She shed her dress, departed, and settled into the suburbs—deaf, mute, crude, and blind—leaving her bowl behind. That empty bowl became mine, along with the ruined dress. Now, though Jim Crow dies, ravens arrive bearing mere crumbs, telling me to eat and be satisfied. Instead, I fast, I pray, and I continue the journey.

---

>
> Measured in the vast distance that Jim Crow flies, the journey spanned oceans and beyond. I resonated with an unstoppable strength, and they could not suppress me for long. My feet were exhausted, my eyes were strained, and my heart was broken from attending to the soiled edges of Miss Liberty Muffet’s attire. Still, I persevered. I traveled a thousand blood-stained miles beyond the reign of Jim Crow on that memorable December day when I sat down beside Miss Muffet of Montgomery. 
>
> I spoke, echoing the familiar refrain: “What is in the bowl, Thief?” I told her, “That is your curse,” and added, “This is my way.” 
>
> She slipped out of her dress, left the scene, and relocated to the suburbs—unresponsive, silent, vulgar, and blind to the reality around her. ***

### The Unyielding Path to Freedom

For decades, the relentless grind of hard labor and the suffocating weight of systemic oppression had claimed my youth and strength. I had spent a lifetime bowing to a society that demanded my endless toil while systematically denying my basic humanity. But beneath the surface of quiet endurance, a profound exhaustion took root—not merely a fatigue of the muscle and bone, but a weariness of the soul. I grew utterly tired of serving a system designed to keep me diminished, and I knew I could no longer participate in my own subjugation.

That bone-deep weariness finally reached its breaking point on a cold, historic December day in Montgomery. As I sat on that city bus, a white woman demanded that I yield my space to her, expecting the immediate, submissive compliance that tradition had dictated for generations. Instead, I remained seated. In that quiet, unwavering refusal, I claimed my right to exist as an equal. The authorities were summoned, and my nonviolent defiance resulted in my forcible arrest, dragged away for daring to occupy my own space.

Though the police physically restrained me and locked me behind iron bars, they were powerless to contain the momentum of that moment. What they mistook for an isolated incident of insubordination was, in truth, the spark that ignited a long-dormant fire. My act of defiance echoed far beyond the walls of that Montgomery jail, surging across the nation to ignite an unstoppable wave of resistance. Millions recognized their own pain in my refusal, and together, we transformed a single act of courage into a powerful, unyielding movement for civil rights.

Confronted by this unprecedented moral force, the white oppressor saw her unearned privilege and unquestioned authority begin to crumble. Unable to maintain her dominance in the face of our unified strength, she gradually abandoned her position, retreating from the integrated public square and into the sterile isolation of suburban flight. In seeking safety behind the manicured lawns of suburban exile, she left behind an empty legacy—a hollow system built on prejudice, shattered by the very people it had sought to oppress.

Yet, the dismantling of Jim Crow and the removal of segregation signs were never the ultimate destination. I refuse to accept superficial concessions, performative gestures, or the mere illusion of progress as a substitute for real justice. True liberation requires more than the absence of overt tyranny; it demands the presence of full equality. Today, my journey continues—a deeply spiritual and fiercely active pursuit of absolute freedom, driven by the conviction that the march toward justice is far from over.

**Title:** The Weight of the Seat: Labor, Defiance, and the Unfinished Revolution

In December of 1955, the city of Montgomery, Alabama, was a landscape defined by the relentless, grinding machinery of Jim Crow. For the city’s Black working class, survival required navigating a daily gauntlet of systemic cruelty, psychological humiliation, and grueling physical labor. Among them was Rosa Parks, a forty-two-year-old Black seamstress whose daily routine was measured in the sharp prick of pins, the monotonous hum of a department store sewing machine, and the heavy ache in her shoulders at the end of a long shift. Yet, the physical exhaustion of her labor was merely a symptom of a deeper, more suffocating fatigue: the soul-weariness born of surviving under a caste system designed to strip Black men and women of their fundamental humanity. 

On the evening of December 1, as Parks boarded the Cleveland Avenue bus to return home, she entered a space that functioned as a daily microcosm of racial terror. In Montgomery, the public transit system was tailored to enforce white supremacy. Black passengers paid their fares at the front, were forced to step off the bus, and reboarded through the back door; inside, they were subjected to the whims of white drivers who routinely hurled verbal abuse or pulled away before Black riders could reenter. On this particular evening, as the bus filled, the driver demanded that Parks and three other Black passengers surrender their seats in the "colored" section so that a white man could sit down. 

The myth that emerged in later decades painted Rosa Parks as merely a quiet woman with tired feet. In truth, her feet were no more tired than usual. What had reached its limit was her endurance of an unjust social order. Parks’s fatigue was historical, structural, and political. As a seasoned secretary for the local NAACP chapter who had investigated cases of systemic sexual violence and racial terror against Black people, she understood the precise mechanics of white privilege. Thus, when she refused to stand, her act was not a passive retreat into tiredness, but a deliberate, quiet, and unwavering confrontation with a regime of terror. 

By remaining seated, Parks leveraged the profound economy of stillness against the violence of white supremacy. Her simple, calm "No" shattered the illusion of Black acquiescence that Jim Crow required to function. She took her seat not as a posture of rest, but as a claim to ownership over her own body, dignity, and citizenship. 

Her subsequent arrest was meant to enforce the status quo; instead, it served as the catalyst that unraveled it. Parks’s quiet defiance ignited a long-burning fire within Montgomery’s Black community. The resulting Montgomery Bus Boycott—a 381-day masterclass in strategic, collective action—saw tens of thousands of working-class Black citizens walk, share rides, and brave economic reprisal and physical violence rather than submit to the indignity of segregated buses. The economic power of Black labor, once exploited by the city, was now weaponized against it. 

The boycott culminated in the landmark Supreme Court decision in *Browder v. Gayle*, which declared segregated public buses unconstitutional. Parks’s singular act had forced the legally sanctioned apparatus of white supremacy to retreat, proving that the legal walls of Jim Crow were not impenetrable.

However, the fall of *de jure* segregation was a victory, not a final resolution. While the legal victory dismantled the formal architecture of Jim Crow in public transit, it left behind an unfulfilled legacy. The retreat of explicit legal segregation did not automatically erase the deep-seated economic disparities, residential segregation, institutional violence, and subtle forms of racial hierarchy that continued to plague the nation. The destruction of the law did not immediately transform the hearts, minds, or economic structures built on centuries of exploitation. 

The story of Rosa Parks serves as both a monument and a reminder. It demonstrates that while structural legal changes are vital, the fall of explicit oppression does not mark the end of the struggle for true liberation. The journey toward total freedom is an ongoing process that demands persistent spiritual fortitude and physical resistance. The work initiated by a seamstress taking her seat on a Montgomery bus remains unfinished; it lives on in every generation that refuses to yield its dignity, reminding us that liberation is not a static gift granted by the powerful, but a continuous practice of courageous defiance.

There are some memories that time simply cannot erase, no matter how many years slip by. For me, it will always be **that** particular winter—the one where the snow fell so thick and heavy that it seemed to silence the entire world. It was **December**, and the chilly air carried the sharp, cozy scent of burning pine and fresh frost. 

Every afternoon, on my way home from school, I would stop by the town’s tiny, sunlit bakery. Sitting behind the glass counter was **Miss** Clara, a soft-spoken woman with silver hair and a smile that could warm the coldest afternoon. She always set aside a warm cinnamon roll for me, listening patiently as I babbled about my day. To a quiet child, her kindness was a rare and comforting anchor.

Right before Christmas, Miss Clara announced she was moving away to live with her daughter in the countryside. The day she left, the sky was a deep, bruised gray, promising another heavy snowfall. I stood on the platform, waving until the red taillights of the train dissolved into the white blur of the storm. 

Decades have passed, but whenever the calendar turns and the first dusting of snow touches the pavement, I find myself looking back. I still **miss** her gentle presence and the quiet magic she brought into my life. Of all the seasons I have lived through, none has ever left quite the same impression as **that** unforgettable **December**.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, lyrical short story blending the story of Rosa Parks in Montgomery with the nursery rhyme "Little Miss Muffet," exploring themes of labor, exhaustion, and quiet rebellion.
counterfactuals.output:
She sat upon a tuffet of split green vinyl, her thimble-pricked thumbs still humming with the memory of another woman’s hemline. The air inside the Cleveland Avenue bus was thick, curdled like sour milk left too long on a sun-scalded porch. 

All day, her fingers had guided silk and wool beneath the iron foot of the Singer machine, feeding the appetite of a city that demanded to be neat, pressed, and pale. By five in the afternoon, her body felt less like flesh and more like a bundle of dry lavender, pressed flat between the heavy pages of a ledger. In her lap lay her small brown paper sack—her meager portion of curds and whey, the bitter salt of a working woman’s supper, the soft, pale sweat of a day spent bending.

The bus rattled over the cobblestones of Montgomery, a iron centipede lunging through a city woven from invisible threads. It smelled of wet wool, diesel, and centuries of unwashed submission.

Then came the spider.

He did not walk; he dangled from the steering column, suspended by long, unseen strands of law and habit. He wore a cap of dark serge, and his eyes were multi-faceted, reflecting forty different shades of fear. He had eight long, ink-stained fingers resting on the wheel, spinning a geometry that kept the world divided into neat, suffocating squares.

The bus lurched to a halt under a streetlamp that bled pale, milky light onto the asphalt. The spider turned in his swivel seat, his shadow stretching long and thin across the aisle, weaving a dark silk over the passengers in the back.

*“Move,”* the spider clicked, his voice like dry husks rubbing together in a autumn draught. *“Vacate the tuffet. Step down into the dark where the silk is thin.”*

Three others rose. They dissolved like sugar into the shadows of the rear, their movements liquid with ancient obedience, frightened away by the threat of the fangs, the venom of the night court, the sticky web of the wire house.

But Little Miss Muffet stayed.

She did not flinch. She did not scatter like a dry leaf. She looked down at her feet—her feet that had walked through seventy years of mud and grease-slicked linoleum, her feet that were so tired they had rooted through the floorboards, through the rusted chassis of the bus, deep into the warm, red clay of Alabama.

*“Aren’t you afraid?”* the bus hissed, its pneumatic doors breathing in, breathing out, like a lung made of brass and steam. *“The spider sits beside you. He occupies the light.”*

The driver stepped down from his dais, his brass buttons glistening like extra eyes along his chest. He loomed over her seat, a shadow with a coin-changer at his hip that jingled like small, metallic teeth. He waited for the flutter of her skirt, the gasping retreat, the familiar surrender that made the world spin in its predictable, cruel orbit.

Instead, she sank deeper into her tuffet. 

The curds and whey in her lap turned to marble. Her heavy wool coat became a coat of mail, forged in the fires of a thousand quiet, unrecorded indignities. Her exhaustion—a weight that should have crushed her—instead solidified into something primordial and unyielding. It was the heavy, dense core of a dying star.

“No,” she whispered.

It was not a shout. It was a knot tied in the thread. A single, perfect stitch that refused to give way under the tension of the wheel.

The driver twitched, his spindly fingers hovering over the air. He had spun a web out of signs and steel, out of brass tokens and municipal ordinances, yet he had forgotten that silk is fragile, and that a stone cannot be caught in a net.

He looked at her, searching for the frightened girl from the nursery rhyme, the girl who would drop her bowl and run into the grass. But there was no girl here. There was only a woman who had sewn the world together for too long, and who had finally decided to stop cutting the thread.

The bus sat motionless in the street, an insect pinned to a map. Outside, the night air of Montgomery hung suspended, thick as cream, waiting for the web to break.

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a prose poem that reimagines a seamstress in Jim Crow-era Montgomery as a mythic, spider-like entity sitting down next to "Miss Muffet"? Make the language poetic, weary, and visionary.
counterfactuals.output:
The heat in Montgomery does not rise; it settles like warm tallow in the small of the back, thick enough to hold a needle upright in the air. Call me Arachne of the red clay; call me eight-handed, crooked-spined, the woman who swallowed a spool of black thread in 1919 and has been spinning it out of her own lungs ever since. My joints are hums of grease and iron; my thumb is callous-pitted from forty years of guiding stiff wool through the sharp, hungry eye of a Singer machine. 

And here she sits upon her bleached tuffet—a stool of plush velvet in the parlor of the dressmaker’s shop, or perhaps just a bench in the sun where the air smells of magnolias and sulfur. She is all starch and pale linen, sipping her cold milk, her curds and whey, untouched by the grease of the loom or the dirt that raised the cow. She is fragile as a bird’s egg, kept whole by the quiet, invisible work of my knees.

I sit down beside her. I do not ask. My hip bones creak like wooden beams in a storm, and the air between us bends under the weight of my exhaustion. 

Look how she quivers. To her, I am all shadow and impossible limbs, a bundle of dark, twitching legs intruding upon her immaculate geometry. She sees the ghost of a bite in the crook of my elbow; she smells the salt of the cotton field in my skin and mistakes it for poison. She clutches her silver spoon as if it were a shield against the dark, terrified that my proximity will curdle her sweetness, that my black crepe skin will rub off on her petticoats.

She does not know that I made her gown. I hemmed the silk for her cotillion; I stitched the lace that keeps her throat so lily-white; I repaired the heavy wool coats of the men who keep the keys to this city. My spit is in her seams; my sweat is the glue in her hemline. I have built this entire town out of thread spun from my own belly, a vast, shimmering web stretched from the basement laundries to the courthouse dome.

I am too tired to bite her, little girl. I am too weary to suck the marrow from her soft, frightened bones. I only sat to rest my eight feet, to lay down the heaviness of a world that expects me to spin forever without ever taking a seat in the sun. 

Do not drop your spoon, Miss Muffet. Do not run. Look at the sky above us: it is tied together with the very lace I pulled through my bleeding fingers. The web is already finished. You sit in the middle of it, but I hold the strand. And if I tug it—just a little, just a gentle, weary twitch of my thumb—the whole bright, terrible town will unravel at our feet.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a stream-of-consciousness monologue from the perspective of a tired seamstress during the Montgomery bus boycott. Combine Southern vernacular with surreal, elevated imagery of threads, empty bowls, and Jim Crow.
counterfactuals.output:
Treadle, treadle, click-clack, and the bobbin spins round like a little silver moon in a dark drawer. Lord, my arches… my arches feel like somebody took a pair of rusted tailor’s shears and notched 'em right at the bone. Six miles at sunrise, and six miles back under this heavy, bruised twilight. Shoes thin as onion skin. But I ain’t taking that seat. No sir, I ain’t fixin' to sit down where the air turns to ice and sour turnip greens.

Look at this seam. *Push.* Silver pin through the taffeta. Missus Montgomery wants her waist pulled in till she can’t catch a soft breath, wants to look like a glass wasp for the cotillion. But who gonna mend the waist of this whole ruined city? 

Jim Crow sitting up there on the bus driver’s visor, black-feathered and fat-bellied, smelling of sulfur and wet newspaper. He got a iron needle in his beak, picking at my spine, dropping shadow everywhere he fly. He stitched this town together with invisible barbed wire—white lace on one side of the street, coarse, bloody burlap on mine. He thought that basting would hold forever. Thought he double-knotted us in the dark back corners, tucked us away like scrap rags in a basket. 

*Prick.* Ah. Crimson bead on the white hem. Wipe it fast before it sets. 

My kitchen table got nothing on it tonight but an empty yellow bowl. Porcelain staring up at me, wide and hollow, like an unblinking eye. An empty bowl in my house, an empty bowl in Sister Clara’s house, empty bowls all down Jackson Street. We eating air, honey. We drinking cold wind and hot dust. But you know what? That empty bowl feels heavier than a feast. It’s sitting there full of everything we *ain't* giving 'em no more. Full of our dimes. Full of our sore heels. Full of the quiet that comes before a thunderstorm rips the porch roof clean off. We turning them empty bowls upside down and standing on 'em to reach the sky.

Step, press, pull. Step, press, pull.

That’s what walking is. It’s just sewing with your feet. Every footstep today was a black thread pulled tight through the hot asphalt, binding me to Brother Martin, binding me to the chillun walking with their schoolbooks, binding us all to the ghost of old Sojourner. We pulling the stitches out of Jim Crow’s suit. We ripping his coat right down the back seam. Hear it pop? *Snap. Snap.* That’s the thread yielding. That’s his iron wire twisting up and snapping in two.

Hands so stiff I can barely thread this eye. Silver eye, so small, but it holds the whole world if you look through it right. My fingers look like tree roots dug out of the red clay, calloused and pricked till the skin’s like old leather thimbles. My body’s just an old ragbag tonight, worn thin at the elbows, stuffed with wool and ache. But my spirit… oh, my spirit is stiff-starched crinoline. It won't bend. It won't crumple. 

Let them yellow buses roll by empty, sounding like hollow tin cans rolling down a hill. Let the vinyl seats dry up and split in the sun. We walking the new cloth now. We cutting out a pattern that ain't never been seen in Alabama. 

Treadle, treadle. Sunlight’s all gone. Just me, the needle, and the dark. My feet are burning like paraffin lamps, but Lord... Lord, they sure do light up the road ahead.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Reinterpret the Civil Rights movement through a dark, allegorical fairytale lens where a seamstress confronts a modern "Miss Muffet" on a bus, turning a simple refusal to move into a mythic judgment.
counterfactuals.output:
In the year the sky turned the color of bruised plums and the city ran on iron and ancient cruelties, the Great Carriage rolled through the rain. It was a beast of black steel, belching coal-smoke, divided neatly down its spine by an invisible, wicked spell. 

In the front sat those born of porcelain and milk, cradled in velvet. In the back, crammed into the shadows, sat the weavers, the diggers, the mothers, and the mendings-men—those whose blood kept the kingdom’s gears turning, though they were forbidden to touch the light.

Among them sat the Seamstress. 

Her fingers were scarred by a thousand needle-pricks, her dark skin stained with indigo dye, her back heavy with the weariness of a thousand unthanked dawns. In her lap lay a wicker basket filled with silver needles and black thread. She was not a queen, nor a sorceress, but she carried the silent weight of a Fate.

The carriage lurched to a halt at the edge of the Gilded Square. 

Boarding the beast came Little Miss Muffet. 

She was a creature of spun-sugar and unearned softness, draped in petticoats that had never known dust. She held a silver cup of curds and whey—sweet, curdled things skimmed from the labor of the shadowed folk. She glided down the aisle, her eyes blue and empty as winter glass, expecting the world to flatten itself into a carpet beneath her slippers.

She stopped before the Seamstress.

Miss Muffet did not speak to her as one speaks to a person. She gasped, a delicate, practiced horror, as though she had found an unsightly insect perched upon her garden wall. She gestured with her silver spoon toward the rear of the carriage, toward the darker shadows where the beasts were meant to crouch.

"Vacate the tuffet," the Driver bellowed from the front. He was a creature of brass buttons and iron jaws, a hound trained to enforce the Kingdom’s decree. "Make way for the pristine. Shrink yourself, shadow-woman."

In the old stories, the spider flees when Miss Muffet recoils. In the old stories, the dark things scatter before the pale and fragile.

The Seamstress looked up. 

She looked at Miss Muffet’s immaculate white gloves, dipped in the blood of invisible labor. She looked at the silver cup of stolen sweetness. She looked at the Driver, whose eyes were hollow gears.

And then, the Seamstress did something that shattered the architecture of the Realm.

She sat still. 

She did not bow her head. She did not weep. She did not rise. 

She simply said, "No."

It was not a shout. It was a word forged in the furnace of three hundred years of silence. The moment it left her lips, the spell that held the carriage together began to fracture.

The rain outside ceased mid-fall, suspended in the air like glass beads. The hum of the carriage engine died, replaced by a deep, resonant vibration that rose from the earth beneath the floorboards. 

Miss Muffet blinked, her delicate mouth agape. "You... you must move," she whispered, her voice quavering, suddenly sounding less like a lady and more like a spoiled child playing in a ruined palace. "It is the Law of the Realm."

"Your law is a fraying garment," the Seamstress said. Her voice was slow, thick with the rustle of dry leaves and ancient loom-shuttles. "It was sewn with rotten thread. And tonight, it unravels."

The Seamstress reached into her wicker basket and pulled forth a single, long strand of black thread. She did not lift a weapon; she merely held the thread between her thumbs. 

To Miss Muffet, the thread suddenly appeared as vast as a horizon, stretching out into the dark, binding her to every lie her ancestors had told. The Seamstress was no longer a tired woman on a bus; she had become the Great Weaver, the ancient creature that lives in the dark corners of the world, sitting patiently while the arrogant build their fragile webs.

Miss Muffet looked down at her silver cup. The curds had turned to ash; the whey had turned to bile. Her pristine white petticoats began to fray at the hem, blackening as if touched by invisible fire.

"Help me!" Miss Muffet shrieked to the Driver, but the Driver was frozen, his hands rusted to the iron steering wheel, his jaw locked in a silent scream. 

"You thought me a spider to be frightened away by your delicate shuddering," the Seamstress murmured, her eyes burning like cold stars in the carriage gloom. "But it is the spider who weaves the web that catches the fly. You have fed on the sweetness of this land for too long, little girl. Now, you shall taste the seat you built for us."

The Seamstress snapped the black thread between her calloused fingers.

A sound like thunder tore through the carriage—not from the sky, but from the hearts of the shadow-folk sitting in the back. One by one, they stood up. They did not raise fists; they simply stood, their shadows lengthening, stretching forward, pouring over the gilded seats, swallowing the pale velvet, washing over Miss Muffet until her bright, painted world was buried beneath a sea of quiet, unstoppable dusk.

Miss Muffet tumbled off her tuffet, scrambling backward on her hands and knees, weeping curds and dust, terrifyingly aware that the world had inverted. The delicate could no longer command the strong.

The bus doors burst open with a groan of dying metal. 

The Seamstress stepped down into the dark, rain-slicked street. She did not look back at the carriage, nor at the trembling creature weeping on the floorboards. Behind her, the shadowy thousands poured out into the night, refusing to ride the iron beast any longer. 

They began to walk. And as their feet struck the pavement, the sound echoed across the kingdom—a rhythmic, mythic marching that shook the towers of glass and bone, unweaving the dark fairytale, thread by bloody thread.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short piece of literary flash fiction inspired by Toni Morrison's style. Mix seamstress terminology, nursery rhymes, and the Montgomery bus incident into a dense, poetic reflection on trauma and freedom.
counterfactuals.output:
Her thumbs were pocked with silver punctures, the skin turned to horn where the needle met the bone. All afternoon she had basted the mayor’s wife’s velvet, smoothing the bias, tucking the waist-darts so the rich red cloth would lie flat against a body that never had to shrink. 

*Baa, baa, black sheep, have you any wool?* 
Yes, sir, yes, sir. Three bolts of crepe, two yards of bone-lace, and a mile of quiet to hem the edges. 

By five o’clock, the sky over Montgomery was the gray of unbleached linen, heavy with rain that refused to drop. She stepped onto the Cleveland Avenue bus, her ankles swollen inside her welted shoes, carrying a weariness that wasn’t in her arches at all, but deep in the weave of her lungs. *London Bridge is falling down, falling down, falling down.* But no bridge fell; only the yellow line painted across the wooden floorboards, a chalked basting stitch dividing the cloth from the remnant.

She sank into the vinyl seat just behind the invisible seam. The leather was cold, unpressed. She closed her eyes, feeling the bobbin of her heart spin back through seventy years of grease-stain and wash-tub work, back to mothers who bled into cotton fields so white folks could wear clean satin. 

The bus lurched. Stop. The driver turned around—a man whose eyes were cut out of hard tailor’s chalk, sharp and pale. His voice came at her like a rusted pair of shears. 

"Move back."

*Rock-a-bye baby, on the treetop. When the wind blows, the cradle will rock.*

The wind had been blowing for three hundred years. The bough had rotted through. Three men stood up to let their freedom be unstitched, but she remained. The trauma was an old thread wound too tight in her chest, pulled past its tension dial until the shuttle shivered. If she yielded now, the whole garment of her soul would pucker. 

"Are you going to stand up?" he asked, the shears opening wide.

She did not look at his face. She looked down at her lap, at her hands resting on her pocketbook—hands that knew how to measure, how to cut, how to mend what had been torn. To move would be to gather the fabric of her dignity and let them trim it to the scrap-heap. To sit was to set her spine like a hot flatiron pressed against wet muslin, steaming out the old, crooked seams of fear.

"No," she said. The word was not a shout; it was a single, unbreakable knot at the end of the line.

*When the bough breaks, the cradle will fall.*

Let it fall, then. Let the basket spill. Let the whole rotten cloth tear down the center. She stayed seated, and in the quiet, dangerous alignment of her bones, the dark heavy world began to unravel.
